content.title: About
content.content: Pork and vegetables, Hawaiian style is a dish that combines tender pork pieces, fresh vegetables (bell pepper, pineapple, carrot) and a fragrant sauce made from soy sauce, ginger and pineapple juice. It is usually stir‑fried quickly in a wok, delivering the sweet‑sour flavor characteristic of Hawaiian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hawaiian cuisine is known for pairing sweet pineapple with meat, giving dishes a tropical aroma.
Traditional Hawaiian dishes often use teriyaki sauce, which adds a sweet‑salty taste.
Pork is one of the most popular meats in the United States, where Hawaiian-style cooking has become widespread.
Pineapple not only adds sweetness but also contains the enzyme bromelain, which helps tenderize meat.
The dish is commonly served over rice or noodles, but can also be used as a filling for tacos.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pork contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper and carrot are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Bromelain from pineapple
items.content: The enzyme bromelain aids digestion and may help reduce inflammation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and ready‑made teriyaki sauce can be high in sodium; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Pineapple allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pineapple or bromelain.

items.title: Overcooking meat
items.content: Excessive stir‑frying can create harmful compounds such as acrylamide and heterocyclic amines.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Certain pork cuts (e.g., shoulder) contain more saturated fat; choosing lean cuts makes the dish healthier.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically over steamed rice, noodles, or as a filling for tacos and burritos. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime juice and toasted sesame seeds for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pork and vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, the dish keeps well for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.
